It gets cheaper if you are a studio.

GLM5.3 is actually not that cheap to run. At least official [Z.Ai](http://Z.Ai) pricing is 1.4/4.4 so it's still going to actually run you at around $35-45/hour in a larger project. If you are a solo developer that really only gets like 2 hours of continuous use - well, that's mere $1500 a month (2 hours, 22 workdays a month). Or $18000 a year. That's true - with utilization this low spending on hardware that can run it is ridiculous. 

But what if you are averaging 16 hours a day? Oh, now it's $560/day, $12300 a month, $150,000 a year. 

Suddenly that $100,000 DGX Station no longer feels ridiculous.

The biggest blocker to affordability isn't hardware level (there are cheaper ways like 512GB Mac Studios), it's utilization. 

If you can reach 24 hours continuous hardware is better than paying for API access. Imho a must have if you are building a game that relies on LLMs (like, say, recently "teaching my little sister how to drive" which really is more of a cautionary tale of why we don't plug OAI keys into a product that can become viral).

replies.author: RandomCSThrowaway01
replies.body:
Yes, actually. Assuming you have ANY kind of gaming PC - go upgrade to 64GB of RAM. Then use Strata and Unsloth Qwen 3.8 Next at Q3 quantization.

With 64GB RAM + 16GB VRAM you can run around 60 TPS and 128k context and at least benchmarks are showing performance comparable to Sonnet 5 in programming. It can actually code, does decent research, will happily do ANY simpler task there is. It likes to think for a while but honestly it's an amazing model (no, seriously, it shits on last year frontier) given it runs on a regular ass computer. One catch is that it will also take all available resources on your PC so you do need to use something else for anything beyond basic chat.

Disclaimer - when I say 'amazing' I don't mean compared to current frontier. No, it will not make you 3D assets in Blender, its vision capabilities are minimal. No, it will not one shot you GTA and no, it's not great at reverse engineering. But it can add smaller features by itself to an existing codebase or one shot stuff like mini games (eg. it won't fail at making a chess engine level of difficulty). 

If it's a whole PC for 1 grand then that's a lot harder sadly. You can run some Gemma and Qwen MoE models but honestly they are meh. Imho a waste of money.

Recommended config nowadays would be 64GB DDR5 + RX 9070 / RTX 5070Ti since that's the lowest to run 3.8 Next at a decent quant and speeds. Followed by 96GB Mac Studio Ultra (since this gives you usable 96GB @ 1.2TB/s), followed by 256GB Mac Studio Ultra (at which point you can run GLM5.3 Flash at 4 bit or maybe Deepseek V4.1 at 2 bit).

I do agree with the person above though - big happy setups do want few hundred thousand USD so you can run big fat GLM 5.3 (technically Q4 fits on 512GB Mac Studio and it won't be THAT bad of an experience). Which is impossible on a personal budget but it's a different story for even a middle sized company.

replies.author: RealSuperdau
replies.body:
This post reads about 3 years out of date.

The benchmarks in the new AA suite have private evaluation sets to prevent benchmaxxing and the US companies clamped down on distillation, that's what's changed.

replies.author: stddealer
replies.body:
Private evaluation sets so that nobody can reproduce the results nor attest the tests are not purposefully biased to fit certain models specific abilities. 

Yes Chinese models are benchmaxxing, and so are American models. Having good benchmark scores is how you advertise your models. Rigging benchmarks is another way to get good scores, arguably worse than benchmaxxing.

replies.author: Deto
replies.body: So you just assume they're rigged without any evidence?

replies.author: stddealer
replies.body:
I'm not saying they're definitely rigged, but it's hard to ignore the pattern: Artificial Analysis seems to consistently update their benchmark aggregate recipe every time a Chinese model gets too close to the top of their leaderboard. Those updates consistently hit OpenAI and Anthropic models less negatively than everyone else. 

And now the new index scores can't even be replicated by an independent third party since they rely on private benchmarks. Plus this update has hurt open weights models even more than any previous one. That also happens to coincide with Anthropic's IPO timing. Maybe I'm seeing conspiracies where there aren't any, but it looks fishy to me

replies.author: Deto
replies.body: Wouldn't you expect the same thing if the open weight models are actually training on the benchmarks, though?

replies.author: stddealer
replies.body: Maybe in some cases, but not when they update the aggregate weights without changing the benchmarks they rely on.

replies.author: Deto
replies.body: oh yeah, that's a little fishy unless they gave a clear/reasonable justification for the specific weight updates.  Definitely could be a post-hoc reasoning issue (e.g., these metrics are bad because they showed something we don't agree with so we down-weighted them).

replies.author: RealSuperdau
replies.body:
Questions are obviously adverserially selected against more or less all currently existing models. Hence why all models score about 0-10% when new frontier benchmarks are released.

replies.author: stddealer
replies.body: Biasing towards one model is not that hard, just do a first run to see which questions the model does good at and remove all the others from the set. Plus this is an aggregate score so you can tweak the weights to favor the things the model is good at and make the others less relevant.

Distilled models, to an extent, are benchmaxxed because they rely on the "curriculum" given to them to learn. If a topic is not in that curriculum, they do worse. That's why known distilled models, Chinese models or known distilled private models, do poorly on new benchmarks or tasks.

And sure I get not trusting AA by itself. But the results for chinese models are, in general, consistent across different testers.

I'll bet that as China gets to understand AA's new benchmarks that they will climb the ranks again. But ultimately, if they don't move away from heavy distillation they won't be as flexible as the frontier American models

replies.author: RuinousFate
replies.body:
Because they don't need to train the same way the US does. They take the work and distill it which is far cheaper and more efficient. Thats why Kimi K3/Deepseek think they are Claude in some calls... because they were routing those calls to Claude and getting back the results for their own training.

  
A simplification is you studying the notes of someone who listened in class and organized and optimized it. You can learn far more efficiently from a time commitment perspective if you have access to those notes compared to the person who did all the work to generate those notes.

  
Also why CN models are forever behind. They don't innovate, they just try to get as much as they can out of that earlier work. For my example, the person who made the notes understands the topic far better.

Now change time for money and you can understand why the CN models are cheaper. Their training costs are cheaper and they don't need to make that all back. 

  
For the margins you are talking about, those margins are similar to US AI models on their API as well. But it's true they do have advantages over US models, some innate (China is cheaper overall lmao), some with obvious trade offs (their models have less parameters) and some just outright being efficiency improvements over US models.

That said, when it comes to being cheap, it's not like the US doesn't have options too. OpenAI's Luna model is basically extremely cheap (cheaper than even Deepseek Flash 4.0 iirc) and completely mogged Deepseek Flash 4.0. 4.1 is better than Luna but also 3x the cost.
